paper_metadata.title: Oxidation resistance and mechanical properties of Laves phase reinforced Cr in-situ composites

evidence.quote: Two-phase Cr( X)–Cr2X (X=Nb, Ta) in-situ composites are of interest for high-temperature applications due to their high melt- ing points and potential for high-temperature strength.
Alloys based on the Cr–Ta system near the Cr(Ta)–Cr 2Ta eutectic exhibited superior oxidation resistance compared to corresponding alloys based on the Cr– Nb system.

Intermetallic alloys based on Cr 2X (X=Nb, Ta, Zr, Hf, etc.) type Laves phases are candidate materials for high-temperature (>900 C) applications due to their high melting points and potential for high-temperature strength [1,2].

phases_and_microstructures.name: nitridation
phases_and_microstructures.material_state: oxidized at 1100°C for 120 h in humid laboratory air

evidence.quote: EPMA analysis revealed two–distinct layers of subscale formation in Cr–10Nb (regions A and B in Fig. 5b). In the first layer (region A), both the Cr(Nb) and Laves phases were nitrided. Vicker’s microhardness measurements showed that this nitridation resulted in extensive hardening ( 1700 VHN) and embrittlement of the Cr(Nb) phase to a depth of approximately 80–100 mm (Fig. 6), more than double that observed in the pure Cr sample shown in Fig. 4.

mechanisms.name: selective nitridation of Laves phase
mechanisms.material_state: oxidized at 1100°C for 120 h in humid laboratory air

evidence.quote: A key finding of this work was that the Cr 2X Laves phase in both alloys was nitrided to a much greater depth than the Cr( X) phase. This was a contributing factor to the relative lack of nitrogen embrittlement of the Cr(Ta) phase in Cr–10Ta (Figs. 7 and 8).

mechanisms.name: Laves phase gettering of nitrogen
mechanisms.material_state: oxidized at 1100°C for 120 h in humid laboratory air

evidence.quote: The Cr 2Ta Laves phase acted as a sink for nitrogen and effectively gettered the relatively small (compared to pure Cr and Cr–10Nb) flux of nitrogen that passed through the scale.
Brittle cleavage frac- ture was observed in the primary Cr(Ta) regions in Cr–8Ta (Fig. 10a) and in the primary Cr 2Ta regions in Cr–11Ta (Fig. 10b).
